bvaAppeals.title: Board of Veterans' Appeals (Parts 19 & 20)
bvaAppeals.description: The Board of Veterans' Appeals (BVA) is the highest level of appeal within the VA system. Understanding these rules is critical if your claim is denied.

categories.title: Understanding BVA Appeals
categories.description: What the Board is and how it works

regulations.title: Rule 1 - Board of Veterans' Appeals
regulations.summary: The Board of Veterans' Appeals is the component of VA that decides appeals. Board members are attorneys appointed by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs.
keyPoints: BVA members are attorneys experienced in veterans law
Board decisions carry the same legal weight as VA regional office decisions
The Board reviews the entire record, not just new evidence
Board hearings allow you to present your case directly
regulations.veteranTip: A BVA appeal is your chance to have an attorney-level review of your entire case. If you've been denied multiple times at the regional office, the Board often sees things differently.

regulations.title: Rule 2 - Board Jurisdiction
regulations.summary: The Board has jurisdiction to decide all questions of law and fact necessary to decide appeals properly before it.
keyPoints: Board can overturn regional office decisions
Board decides both factual and legal questions
Board can remand cases back to the regional office for more development
Board decisions can be appealed to the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims
regulations.veteranTip: Unlike Higher-Level Review, the Board can consider NEW evidence and hold hearings. This is often your best option for complex cases.

categories.title: Appeal Docket Options (AMA)
categories.description: The three dockets available when appealing to the Board

regulations.title: Rule 200 - Notice of Disagreement
regulations.summary: To initiate a Board appeal, you must file a Notice of Disagreement (NOD) on VA Form 10182 within one year of the decision you're appealing.
keyPoints: Must use VA Form 10182 (Decision Review Request: Board Appeal)
Must be filed within 1 year of the decision
Must select one of three docket options
Can specify which issues you're appealing
regulations.veteranTip: When filing a Board appeal, you must choose your docket at the time of filing. Choose carefully - each has different advantages.

regulations.title: Three Docket Options
regulations.summary: Under the Appeals Modernization Act (AMA), you choose one of three dockets when filing a Board appeal.
keyPoints: Direct Review: Fastest, based only on existing record, no new evidence
Evidence Submission: Submit additional evidence within 90 days, no hearing
Hearing Request: Present testimony to a Board member, submit evidence
regulations.veteranTip: Hearing Request is often best for complex cases where you can explain your situation. Direct Review is fastest if you believe the evidence already proves your case.

docketDetails.name: Direct Review Docket
docketDetails.description: Board reviews existing record only. No new evidence, no hearing.
docketDetails.bestFor: Clear cases where evidence already supports claim but was misread
docketDetails.limitation: Cannot add ANY new evidence after filing

docketDetails.name: Evidence Submission Docket
docketDetails.description: Submit additional evidence within 90 days of NOD. No hearing.
docketDetails.bestFor: Cases where you have specific new evidence to submit
docketDetails.limitation: Must submit all evidence within 90 days

docketDetails.name: Hearing Request Docket
docketDetails.description: Testify before a Veterans Law Judge. Can submit evidence at hearing.
docketDetails.bestFor: Complex cases, credibility issues, or cases needing explanation

categories.title: Board Hearings
categories.description: Your right to testify before a Veterans Law Judge

regulations.title: Rule 700 - General Hearing Rules
regulations.summary: A hearing on appeal is a proceeding where you present your case to a Veterans Law Judge. You may appear in person or via video conference.
keyPoints: Hearings are optional but can be very helpful
In-person hearings held at VA Central Office in Washington, D.C.
Video hearings available at local VA regional offices
Virtual tele-hearings available from your home
You may bring witnesses to testify
regulations.veteranTip: Video and virtual hearings are just as effective as in-person hearings. The judge focuses on your testimony, not where you're sitting.

regulations.title: Rule 701 - Right to a Hearing
regulations.summary: You have the right to a hearing before the Board decides your appeal. The hearing must be requested when filing the NOD.
keyPoints: Must request hearing on VA Form 10182
Can submit written statement instead of hearing
Witnesses can testify on your behalf
Hearing transcript becomes part of the record
regulations.veteranTip: If you're good at explaining your symptoms and their impact on your life, a hearing can be very persuasive. Judges often grant claims after hearing testimony directly from veterans.

regulations.title: Rule 717 - Submitting Evidence
regulations.summary: At a Board hearing, you may submit additional evidence. Evidence submitted at the hearing is automatically accepted into the record.
keyPoints: Can submit new evidence at the hearing
Evidence must be relevant to the issues on appeal
Board member may ask questions about the evidence
Written brief summarizing your case is helpful
regulations.veteranTip: Bring organized copies of your key evidence to the hearing. A brief written statement summarizing your argument helps the judge understand your case.

categories.title: Board Decisions & What Happens Next
categories.description: Understanding Board decisions and further appeal options

regulations.title: Board Decision Outcomes
regulations.summary: The Board can grant your appeal, deny it, or remand it back to the regional office for additional action.
keyPoints: Grant: Board rules in your favor - you win
Denial: Board upholds the original decision
Remand: Board sends case back for more development or new exam
Partial Grant/Denial: Some issues granted, others denied
regulations.veteranTip: A remand is NOT a denial. It means the Board found problems with how VA handled your case. Remands often lead to grants after the regional office fixes the errors.

regulations.title: Rule 904 - Reconsideration
regulations.summary: You may request the Board reconsider its decision if there was obvious error or if you have new evidence that could change the outcome.
keyPoints: File motion for reconsideration with the Board
Must show obvious error in the decision
New evidence can support reconsideration
No time limit, but file promptly
regulations.veteranTip: Reconsideration is rare but can work if the Board clearly made a factual or legal mistake in your decision.

regulations.title: Appeal to Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims
regulations.summary: If the Board denies your appeal, you can appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims (CAVC) within 120 days.
keyPoints: Must file Notice of Appeal within 120 DAYS (strict deadline)
CAVC reviews legal errors, not factual disputes
Can represent yourself or hire an attorney
Many cases settled through Joint Motion for Remand
regulations.veteranTip: The 120-day deadline for CAVC appeals is ABSOLUTE - there are almost no exceptions. If you're considering CAVC, consult an accredited attorney immediately.
regulations.importantWarning: The 120-day CAVC deadline is one of the strictest in all of federal law. Missing it by even one day means you cannot appeal.

pension.title: VA Pension Benefits (38 CFR Part 3 Subpart D)
pension.description: Non-service-connected pension benefits for wartime veterans with limited income and permanent total disability.
pension.note: Pension is DIFFERENT from disability compensation. It's for veterans who are disabled (not from service) and have financial need.

categories.title: Pension Eligibility Basics
categories.description: Who qualifies for VA pension benefits

regulations.title: Pension Overview
regulations.summary: VA pension is a needs-based benefit for wartime veterans who have limited income and are either 65+ or permanently and totally disabled (not necessarily from service).
keyPoints: NOT the same as disability compensation
Based on financial need, not service connection
Requires wartime service (specific periods defined)
Must be permanently and totally disabled OR age 65+
Income and net worth limits apply
regulations.veteranTip: If you have disabilities that aren't service-connected but still prevent you from working, pension may provide monthly income even without proving service connection.

regulations.title: Wartime Service Periods
regulations.summary: To qualify for pension, you must have served during a recognized wartime period.
keyPoints: World War II: Dec 7, 1941 - Dec 31, 1946
Korean Conflict: June 27, 1950 - Jan 31, 1955
Vietnam Era: Feb 28, 1961 - May 7, 1975 (varies by location)
Gulf War: Aug 2, 1990 - date to be determined (ongoing)
regulations.veteranTip: You don't need to have served IN the war zone - just during the wartime period. Many veterans don't realize they qualify as 'wartime veterans.'

regulations.title: Basic Pension Entitlement
regulations.summary: A veteran meets the service requirements for pension if they served 90 days or more during wartime (or were discharged for service-connected disability before 90 days).
keyPoints: Minimum 90 days of active service during wartime
At least one day of wartime service required
Discharge under conditions other than dishonorable
Exception for service-connected disability discharge
regulations.veteranTip: If you served even one day during a wartime period with at least 90 days total service, you may meet the wartime service requirement.

categories.title: Aid & Attendance and Housebound
categories.description: Enhanced pension rates for veterans needing assistance

regulations.title: Aid and Attendance (A&A)
regulations.summary: Veterans receiving pension may qualify for additional Aid and Attendance benefits if they need help with daily activities like bathing, dressing, or eating.
keyPoints: Higher pension rate for those needing daily assistance
Includes help with activities of daily living (ADLs)
Can also qualify if blind or in nursing home
Significantly increases monthly pension amount
regulations.veteranTip: If you receive pension and need help from another person for daily tasks, apply for Aid & Attendance. It can increase your monthly benefit by over $1,000.

regulations.title: Housebound Benefits
regulations.summary: Veterans who are substantially confined to their home due to disability may qualify for housebound pension rate.
keyPoints: Lower rate than A&A but still increases pension
For veterans substantially confined to home
Can qualify with single permanent disability rated 100%
Also requires additional disability(ies) rated 60%+
regulations.veteranTip: Housebound is easier to qualify for than Aid & Attendance. If you rarely leave home due to your disabilities, you may qualify.

regulations.title: Countable Income
regulations.summary: Pension is reduced dollar-for-dollar by countable income. Certain medical expenses can be deducted from income.
keyPoints: Most income counts: Social Security, retirement, wages
Unreimbursed medical expenses reduce countable income
Pension = Maximum Rate minus Countable Income
If income exceeds maximum rate, no pension payable
regulations.veteranTip: Keep ALL receipts for medical expenses - medications, doctor visits, medical equipment, health insurance premiums. These reduce your countable income and increase your pension.

regulations.title: Net Worth Limitation
regulations.summary: VA considers your net worth (assets) when determining pension eligibility. Excessive net worth can disqualify you even if income is low.
keyPoints: Net worth limit is approximately $150,538 (adjusted annually)
Primary residence excluded from net worth
Personal property and one vehicle generally excluded
Look-back period for asset transfers
regulations.veteranTip: Your house and one car don't count toward net worth. If you're close to the limit, consult with an accredited attorney about legal ways to become eligible.
